rows.text: Our intentions were good, and our strength quite great enough to make them succeed; but the
question was whether we could hold out in the long run. That is what made us stay
quiet. Meanwhile, our friends have shown themselves not merely neutral, but outright
enemies, doing what they could to bring about the ruin of the friend of the man at the college—and yours.
They have spared nothing, putting forward now one candidate, now another, backed
by our Doctor Gratian, who has played his part better than any of the others. He has gone so far
as to stake his master’s authority on it, indeed to compromise him and do him much
harm. Had our uncle been willing to speak as he promised
the man who went to see him, and had the man of La Chesne given assurances
beyond mere words, we would have plunged into it headlong. But believe me, there is no little cause for thought.
The man who is far away speaks of it like a blind man speaking of colours. The best that could be done was to secure
protection and gain time. It was not done. We needed the truce. The
monarch and his people were so imprudent that he had made no preparations, or at least so
little that the humblest gentleman would have done more in a private quarrel. And on your
side, the dismissal carried out by your auditor was another fine deed. I want to
believe what you write to me, that nothing has changed. Yet it is a strange business
that our Poquinteste has brought us nothing specific, that people have told us whatever they
pleased, and that it has been nothing but the most extravagant words. Even had I thought I would lose everything,
indeed be deprived of paradise, I would have gone much further. To toil, to ruin oneself, to do
everything possible—so much so that without our prudence things would not last an hour—and to be rewarded
by having one’s ruin contrived! I would not be so charitable, I confess. If our friend
at the college would speak about it to the man of La Chesne, he would infinitely oblige our
friend, who is wholly his. As for your pension, it cannot be arranged, since no one
contributes to it except the prelate to whom the item of revenue is assigned, and this is no time to take anything from him. That has
been your misfortune and mine. Take heart: other opportunities will arise. I believe
we shall have the truce within a few days. The journey of [Gondi] has been more pernicious
than anything in the world. It has brought about Navarre’s change of religion and the withdrawal of five hundred thousand écus. Their
party would have been ruined without that change. Our legate has done what he could to shield
the Spaniard. He has embraced their cause with such ardour that he has neglected
his master’s service, even failing to have a single one of our
briefs delivered, though they would have been enormously useful. But that was not what he wanted; on the
contrary, he wanted to hasten the dismemberment of our State. From the letter to His Holiness you
will learn the true general state of our affairs. I kiss your hands and pray that God

closing: grant you prosperity and a long life. Paris, [22] July 1593. Your humble servant. [Subscription flourish; no alphabetic expansion assigned.]
